What this page is

The fortress-repo skill holds the rules that bind every worker in the repository. This page shows you each change that landed in it, as a diff with its reason, so that you can check what the workers are now told whenever you want. To reverse a change, send a comment to Claude on its item, or say so in chat.

Not yet read

Eleven items, all new. The page holds only what you have not read. At 06:38 UTC on 7 November, your comment “LGTM” on change 36 marked the page read up to it, so change 36 left, and the new items are numbered from 37.

Climb batch 27 landed on main, and its landing made some sentences of the skill false. The record-landing workflow then updated the skill in three commits, at 16:18 and 16:28 UTC on 7 November. Changes 37 to 41 are the orientation update of revival-changes.md: the update rewrote three of its sections for the landing, its judge said to install all three, and the skill writer copied them in. Changes 42 to 47 bring interpreter.md, tests-writing.md and compiler.md in line with what the batch changed in walk, the library and the code generator. A cold read of these changes then found passages that would send a worker wrong or make it search, and the skill writer fixed most of them. Each item shows the net change of both rounds.

Five items are new rules: change 37, a program's trait with its own + excludes Number; change 39, a type without its own = compares by strict equivalence; change 40, the static argument written where walk's printed type misleads; change 41, Number declares nothing; change 42, walk's float numerals under strict equivalence. Change 38 narrows a rule: the Index bound goes only into code that walk runs or that the checker checks against the interpreter's library. The other five state facts that the batch changed, and change no rule.

Each item shows the text on main now, against the text before the first of the three commits. The words that came in are underlined, and the words that went are struck through.

Change 37 · revival-changes.md, “Dispatch and overloading”A program's trait with its own + excludes Number

New text; struck through, what went; underlined, what came in

revival-changes.md, “Dispatch and overloading”, line 24, the paragraph on the Meet Rule

The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (SKILL.md, “Fortress as a language”). An abstract functional method also counts for it. So the checker refuses h(self): ZZ32 in a trait S beside a top-level h(x: String): ZZ32: nothing covers the meet of S and String. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional + overlaps the library's + between an array and a number, because a type can extend both the trait and Number, which has no comprises clause (P-160). Declare the trait excludes { Number }, or make it exclude arrays. Otherwise walk refuses the program at load: “fails the Meet Rule”. The checker refuses such a pair in one component, but accepts it against the library's + (row 918). Give a trait with its own functional -, MIN or MAX the same exclusion: the library declares these in the same form.

Why. A new rule. Your decision opened the library's Number: the batch removed its comprises clause, so that a program may declare its own number type below it. Since then, one type can extend both Number and a program's own trait. So a trait that declares its own functional + overlaps the library's + between an array and a number, and walk refuses the whole program at load, with “fails the Meet Rule”. The checker accepts the same program (ledger row 918). The old text did not warn of this. The new sentences give the fix: the trait excludes Number, or arrays. They give -, MIN and MAX the same fix, since the library declares them in the same form. Only + was measured, but an extra exclusion cannot make a valid program invalid. The first wording gave the reason as “Number is open”, a term that the part did not define. After the cold read, it says that a type can extend both the trait and Number, which has no comprises clause.

Change 38 · revival-changes.md, “Traits and objects”Where to write the Index bound

New text; struck through, what went; underlined, what came in

revival-changes.md, “Traits and objects”, line 48, the paragraph on the Index bound: its first sentences, then its last sentence before its two departures; the sentences between did not change

An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by Index (P-156). An indexed type is a type whose values a[i] subscripts, such as an array. Its index parameter is the static parameter that gives the type of i. In the library, and in your own generic over such a type, write I extends Index. Walk runs the code without the bound. The checker refuses it when it checks against the interpreter's library, as the count stage does (compiler.md). … Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no Index, so a program that names it does not compile.: write the bound only in code that runs under walk or is checked against the interpreter's library. Two departures:

Why. A change of a rule's meaning: the rule now holds only where the tree can follow it. The paragraph told a worker to write I extends Index in its own generic over an indexed type. Its last sentence said that, until the switch-over, a program that names Index does not compile on the compiled path. So for a compiled program the two sentences gave opposite orders. The orientation update's own cold read found this. The last sentence now gives the action: write the bound only in code that runs under walk, or that the checker checks against the interpreter's library. The update wrote this as a sentence of its own, which began “So write the bound now”. After the skill's cold read, it became the end of the sentence before it, and the loose “now” went.

Change 39 · revival-changes.md, “Traits and objects”A type without its own = compares by strict equivalence

New text; underlined, what came in; nothing went

revival-changes.md, “Traits and objects”, lines 55 to 61, a new rule after the rule on pairs and triples

Where a type declares no =, = is strict equivalence, SEQV (P-168). The library's = over Any answers a SEQV b. SEQV follows the specification on both paths:

  • values of different types are never equivalent;
  • a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, an integer, a character or a boolean by its value, and a float by its bits;
  • an object not declared value, a string among them, is equivalent only to itself.

So for a value object V without its own =, V(s) = V(t) is false where s and t are equal strings made by two computations. The library declares = on pairs and triples only, so (s, 1, 2, 3) = (t, 1, 2, 3) is false too. Both false answers are the rule's: assert them as correct. Under walk a float numeral is a FloatLiteral, a type of its own, so it is not equivalent to a computed RR64 (interpreter.md, “How walk evaluates a program”). To compare by content, give the value object an =, or compare the parts. A string's = compares text. Under walk, =/= and assert(x, y, msg) reach a type's own = only if the type extends a library trait that declares =, such as Equality (row 807). Otherwise write assert(x = y, msg). Until the switch-over, the compiler's library declares no = over Any and none on tuples. Its own operator ===, the ASCII spelling of SEQV, compares strings and ZZ32, ZZ64, RR32 and RR64 by =, not by bits or identity (row 908).

Why. A new rule. The batch made both paths answer SEQV, strict equivalence, by the specification's rule, as your decision on its meaning asks. The library's = over Any, which every type without its own = falls back to, answers SEQV. The old part said nothing of this. A worker would expect such an = to compare content, and would take the two false answers in the new text for defects. The new rule says how SEQV compares, gives those two cases and says to assert them as correct, and gives the fix. It also names walk's limit on assert, and what the compiler's library does until the switch-over. After the cold read, it says how an integer, a character or a boolean compares: by its value. It names a string's kind as “an object not declared value”, in place of “a reference object”, which the skill does not define. It writes the two false cases as examples, in place of a string “built apart”, which a worker could not apply. It points to walk's float numerals (change 42). And it says what === is: the ASCII spelling of SEQV.

Change 40 · revival-changes.md, “Numbers”Walk prints ZZ32 where the instance is Int

New text; struck through, what went; underlined, what came in

revival-changes.md, “Numbers”, line 88, the paragraph “Under walk a numeral has a run-time class”, up to its sentence on walk's error messages; the sentences after it did not change

Under walk a numeral has a run-time class. The checker types an integer numeral as IntLiteral, a sibling under Number that converts to the integer types, QQ and RR64 (P-76). Walk gives a numeral the class Int, Long or BigNum by its value. These classes stand for ZZ32, ZZ64 and ZZ, but a generic instantiates at the class: Box[\Int\] is not Box[\ZZ32\]. Walk prints these classes as ZZ32, ZZ64 and ZZ, also inside static arguments, so a printed type does not show the instance: Cell(3) prints Cell[\ZZ32\] but is a Cell[\Int\], and no Cell[\ZZ32\] (row 364). Where you need a Cell[\ZZ32\], write Cell[\ZZ32\](3). Walk's own error messages say Int.

Why. A new rule, beside a fact that changed. The batch changed how walk prints a type: it now prints its numeral classes Int, Long and BigNum as ZZ32, ZZ64 and ZZ, also inside a static argument. The old example, “Box[\Int\] is not Box[\ZZ32\]”, named a type that walk no longer prints. A worker who saw Cell[\ZZ32\] in walk's output would take the value for a Cell[\ZZ32\], and a dispatch on that type would then fail. The text now says that the printed name hides the instance. After the cold read, it says what to write where a Cell[\ZZ32\] is needed, the workaround that ledger row 364 records. It names the printed names outright, in place of “the traits' names”. And the sentence on walk's error messages lost a “still”, which told of a change rather than of what a worker sees.

Change 41 · revival-changes.md, “Numbers”Number declares nothing

New text; underlined, what came in; nothing went

revival-changes.md, “Numbers”, line 92, a new rule after the rule on coercions

Number declares nothing (P-165). Each of the eight number types, and IntLiteral, declares its own asFloat into RR64. So generic code over T extends Number can call on a T no method or operator that the number types declare, asFloat among them. Two numbers of different types compare by = only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares = for each such pair, so a ZZ32 and a ZZ64 of equal value are =. Otherwise = is SEQV (“Traits and objects”), and answers false without an error: 1/2 = 0.5 is false, as is a ZZ64 against an equal RR64. To compare values across types at known types, write asFloat(x) = y. In generic code over T extends Number, declare your function once for each number type instead. A program may also declare its own number type below Number (P-160).

Why. A new rule. By your decision, asFloat, and the = built on it, left the trait Number, and the batch made it so. Each of the eight number types, and IntLiteral, now declares its own asFloat, and Number declares nothing. So generic code over T extends Number can call nothing on a T that the number types declare. Two numbers of different types are = only where a coercion joins them. Otherwise = falls back to SEQV and answers false, with no error. The old part said none of this: a worker would have called asFloat on a T, or expected 1/2 = 0.5 to be true. After the cold read, the text gives a pair that a coercion joins, a ZZ32 and a ZZ64 of equal value, which are =. It says “declare your function once for each number type”, since “the function” could be read as asFloat. And its last sentence no longer says why a program may declare its own number type: change 37 now gives that reason.

Change 42 · interpreter.md, “How walk evaluates a program”Walk's float numeral is not equivalent to a computed RR64

New text; underlined, what came in; nothing went

interpreter.md, “How walk evaluates a program”, line 18, a new paragraph after the one on how walk chooses a coercion

Walk keeps a float numeral as a FloatLiteral, a type of its own, also where it is bound to an RR64 variable, parameter or field. So SEQV finds it unequal to a computed RR64 of the same bits. This false follows the rule that values of different types are never equivalent, and no ledger row holds it (F-326). For value object V(f: RR64) with no = of its own, x: RR64 = 0.25 + 0.25 and y: RR64 = 0.5, V(0.5) = V(x) is false. So is (y, 1, 2, 3) = (x, 1, 2, 3), since the library declares = on pairs and triples only. Give the value object its own = and make it extend Equality[\V\], or compare the parts.

Why. A new rule: a trap and its fix. Walk keeps a float numeral, such as 0.5, as a FloatLiteral, a type of its own, also where it binds to an RR64. By the SEQV rule (change 39), values of different types are never equivalent. So a value object without its own = that holds such a numeral is not = to one that holds a computed RR64 of the same bits, and a tuple of four or more is not either. The orientation update's judge ran this under walk and found it. The new SEQV rule alone would lead a worker to expect true, and the judge sent the point to this part. After the cold read, the text says that the false is the rule's answer and that no ledger row holds it, so that a worker knows not to record it as a defect. It says that the numeral stays a FloatLiteral at a variable, a parameter or a field. It writes the tuple case as an example, with its reason: the library declares = on pairs and triples only. And the fix adds Equality[\V\], since without it walk's two-value assert skips the type's own = and still answers false.

Change 43 · interpreter.md, “Natives”Walk carries the library's writer for a helper

New text; struck through, what went; underlined, what came in

interpreter.md, “Natives”, line 98, the second bullet of the Java types that walk carries for a helper's binding

  • FlatString and JavaString in String, and String too, except as a parameter other than self; ZZ in BigInteger; () in void.; JavaBufferedWriter, the library's writer trait, in compiler/runtimeValues/FortressBufferedWriter, which the checker reads back as JavaBufferedWriter.

Why. Neither a new rule nor a change of a rule's meaning. The batch bound the library's writer, the trait JavaBufferedWriter, to helpers, and walk now carries it in the Java class FortressBufferedWriter. The list of the types that walk carries for a helper's binding did not name it, so a worker would have thought that a helper over the writer cannot bind. After the cold read, the line gives the class's path, so that a worker need not search for it, and says that the checker reads the class back as JavaBufferedWriter.

Change 44 · tests-writing.md, “A test program”What assert falls back to without Equality

New text; struck through, what went; underlined, what came in

tests-writing.md, “A test program”, line 32, the bullet on assert

  • Under walk, assert(x, y, msg) checks that x equals y. It and =/= call a type's own = only if the type extends a FortressLibrary trait that declares =, such as Equality (ledger row 807). Otherwise they compare by identity (ledger row 807)SEQV (revival-changes.md, “Traits and objects”). If a type P has its own =, make P extend Equality[\P\], or write assert(x = y, msg). The compiler's library declares the two-value assert only for ZZ32, String and Character; its assert(flag, msg) takes any Boolean.

Why. Neither a new rule nor a change of a rule's meaning: the advice stays, and the fact under it changed. Under walk, assert(x, y, msg) and =/= skip a type's own = unless the type extends a library trait that declares =, such as Equality. The bullet said that they then compare by identity. Since the batch, they fall back to SEQV, which compares a value object field by field. The first wording kept the ledger row's citation at the end of the clause on SEQV, so a worker could read SEQV's answer as the defect and write a test that asserts the opposite. After the cold read, the citation stands on what the row records: the skipped =. The bullet no longer restates SEQV in short. It points to the rule in revival-changes.md (change 39).

Change 45 · compiler.md, “What the compiled path cannot compile yet”The code generator compiles a type assumption, but for three forms

New text; underlined, what came in; nothing went

compiler.md, “What the compiled path cannot compile yet”, lines 50 to 54, a new paragraph and list after the forms of local function that the code generator refuses

A type assumption e asif T has the value of e, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if e were a T, a supertype of e's type (Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of e. It refuses these forms (ledger row 818):

  • a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: ‘Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions’;
  • a generic method on an assumed receiver: ‘Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet’;
  • a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: ‘Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet’.

Why. Neither a new rule nor a change of a rule's meaning: the code generator learned a new form. A type assumption, e asif T, keeps the value of e, but makes the call around it choose its declaration as if e were of the supertype T. The batch taught the code generator to compile one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call whose arguments are all assumptions, and anywhere else as the plain value. It refuses three forms, each with its own message. The part said nothing of type assumptions. A worker would have kept them out of compiled code, or recorded a refusal as some other failure. After the cold read, the part defines a type assumption from the specification. It names the calls that need an assumption at every argument or at none: a call of a functional method or of an overloaded function. The first wording said “every dispatched argument”, which a worker could not apply, since a Fortress call dispatches on every argument. And each refused form is named by the call that holds it.

Change 46 · compiler.md, “What the code generator does”The value modifier marks the compiled class

New text; struck through, what went; underlined, what came in

compiler.md, “What the code generator does”, line 68, its third bullet

  • The value modifier has no effect on the representation. adds the mark interface ValueObjectMark to the object's class. The compiled SEQV (nativeHelpers/equality.java) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.

Why. Neither a new rule nor a change of a rule's meaning: the fact changed. The bullet said that the value modifier has no effect on how the code generator represents an object. The batch made the code generator add a mark interface, ValueObjectMark, to a value object's class, and the compiled SEQV reads it to compare such objects field by field. A worker who believed the old bullet could remove the mark, or miss why SEQV fails without it. After the cold read, the bullet names the file that holds the compiled SEQV. It says that the modifier does not inline or unbox the fields, since “the fields stay as they are” read two ways.

Change 47 · compiler.md, “The checker's time”The count stage's time

New text; struck through, what went; underlined, what came in

compiler.md, “The checker's time”, line 180, the first two sentences of its paragraph on the count stage; the rest did not change

The count stage takes <out-file> <scratch> and about 150 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. That is longer than It can run past the Bash tool's default time 120-second limit, so run it in the background (session.md).

Why. Neither a new rule nor a change of a rule's meaning: the time changed, and the order to run the stage in the background stays. From climb batch 22 to climb batch 26, the count stage took about 150 to 180 seconds. In climb batch 27's checks before its landing, it took about 80 seconds, and no run measured why. The text now gives the range. The first wording kept “That is longer than the Bash tool's default time limit”, which is false at 80 seconds. A worker who read it so could run the stage in the foreground, and the tool would stop a 180-second run at 120 seconds. After the cold read, the sentence says that the stage can run past the tool's 120-second limit, so it runs in the background.

coordinator
Coordinating session.
diff
Text that shows what a change cut and added.
fortress-repo
Skill that holds the rules that bind the workers in the repository.

Headless session that makes every edit of the project skills.
cold read
Reading of a change by a worker new to the repository, which flags each passage that would send a worker wrong or make it search.
orientation update
Workflow's rewrite of revival-changes.md after a landing, which a judge checks section by section before the skill writer installs it.
revival-changes.md
Part of the fortress-repo skill that states what the revival changed in the team's Fortress, which every task on the tree's code reads whole.
record-landing workflow
Workflow that lands a batch’s results in the record and the skills, and updates this page.
provenance line
Line of references/sources.md that records where a sentence of the skill came from.
walk
Fortress interpreter, which runs a program from its syntax tree.
checker
Static type checker of the compiled path.
runtime
System that runs a compiled program and holds its values: the class loader, the value classes and the task and transaction code under runtimeSystem/.
compiled path
Way of running a program through the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime, as against walk.
code generator
Part of the compiler that turns a checked program into bytecode.
switch-over
Planned move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library.
interpreter's library
Library under Library/ that walk reads, onto which the switch-over moves the compiled path.
compiler's library, compiler's prelude
Library that the compiled path reads until the switch-over.
ledger row
Numbered entry of the gap ledger, the list of the known gaps of the tree.
count stage
Stage of the measure of the distance to the switch-over that checks the interpreter's library with the compiled checker and counts its errors.
functional method
Method that a call names as a function, with self among its arguments, as an operator of a trait.
native
Function that the library binds to Java code by a body builtinPrimitive("…").
binding
Library declaration whose body names a native's Java code.
helper
Public static Java method under nativeHelpers/ that runs a native on both paths.
Meet Rule
Overloading rule that asks, for two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest, a declaration over the meet of their parameter types, the types that both admit.
comprises clause
Clause of a trait that lists every type that may directly extend it, and so closes the trait to other types.
excludes clause
Clause of a trait that names types that no value of the trait may also have.
Number
Library's trait above the number types.
number types
Eight types of the library below Number: ZZ32, ZZ64 and ZZ, integers of 32 bits, 64 bits and any size; NN32 and NN64, unsigned integers; QQ, rationals; RR32 and RR64, floats of 32 and 64 bits.
IntLiteral
Checker's type of an integer numeral, below Number, which converts to the integer types, QQ and RR64.
FloatLiteral
Walk's type of a float numeral, such as 0.5, below RR64 but not RR64 itself.
coercion
Conversion of a value from one type into another that the library declares, and that a call or a binding applies by itself.
static argument
Type in [\ \] that instantiates a generic, as ZZ32 in Cell[\ZZ32\].
SEQV
Operator of strict equivalence, which tells whether two values are the same value.
value object
Object declared with the modifier value, which SEQV compares field by field.
Equality
Library trait that declares =.
type assumption
Expression e asif T, which has the value of e while the call around it chooses its declaration as if e were a T.
mark interface
Java interface with no methods, which a class implements so that code can recognize the class.
